items.title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
items.source_text: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a…
items.summary: ProofPatch helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid as formalizations change, using targeted kernel questions.

items.title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
items.source_text: Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols. To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the…
items.summary: VerusWeave is a benchmark for proof repair in concurrent Verus programs, targeting coding agents on atomic operations and abstract protocols.

items.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
items.source_text: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we…
items.summary: DAPS is a dependency-aware premise selection method for LLM theorem proving in Lean 4, addressing retrieval skew toward popular lemmas.

items.title: Iris on Indirection Theory: Lightweight Higher-order Ghost State
items.source_text: Today, semantic models of languages with concurrency and higher-order state are constructed using step-indexed predicates over resources and higher-order ghost state. There are two main lines of work for constructing such models. On the one hand, Iris provides these in full generality, at the cost of a large body of mechanised domain theory that is difficult to learn and port to new proof assistants. On the other hand, Indirection Theory is much simpler through the use of ordinary dependent types, but its foundation in separation algebra limits the expressiveness of its resource model…
items.summary: Proposes lightweight higher-order ghost state for semantic models using Indirection Theory with ordinary dependent types, as an alternative to Iris.

items.title: Algebraic World Model: From Exploration to Proofs
items.source_text: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then…
items.summary: Algebraic World Model turns interaction with unknown environments into executable Python hypotheses for formal reasoning, mentioning Lean only as background.

items.title: Hammering with Vampire in Lean
items.source_text: We present Vampire-Hammer, a hammer for the Lean interactive theorem prover that discharges goals using the Vampire automated theorem prover and reconstructs proofs checked by the Lean kernel. Vampire-Hammer uses the Lean-auto framework to process goals and premises before dispatching them to Vampire for proof search. Doing so, we rely on standard TPTP problem formats and annotated TSTP proofs that support proof reconstruction. With a 10-second budget on 196,083 eligible Mathlib theorems, Vampire-Hammer solves 21,158 problems not solved by other evaluated tools within the same budget.
items.summary: Vampire-Hammer is a hammer for Lean that sends goals to the Vampire prover and reconstructs proofs checked by the Lean kernel, solving 21,158 extra Mathlib…

items.title: Semantic Path Orders are Generalized Weighted Path Orders
items.source_text: Monotonic semantic path orders (MSPOs) are powerful reduction orders, but their effective use in theorem proving and termination analysis raises three issues: efficient comparison of terms, ground totality, and a reduction-pair formulation. Inspired by weighted path orders (WPOs), we introduce generalized weighted path orders (GWPOs) which encompass both WPOs and MSPOs. GWPOs and MSPOs coincide as classes of reduction orders, thereby yielding efficient and ground-total subclasses of MSPOs. We further formulate the reduction-pair version of the GWPO for the dependency pair method, from which…
items.summary: Introduces generalized weighted path orders that coincide with monotonic semantic path orders, giving efficient ground-total reduction orders for theorem…

items.title: Construction and formal verification of a special topology on {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}: characterization of connected subsets
items.source_text: We examine whether the integers admit a topology whose connected subsets are precisely the sets of consecutive integers. The main result gives a construction for every integer lattice {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, n>0; the answer for Z is then obtained as a corollary. We prove that the neighborhoods determined by the parity of the sum of the coordinates form a basis and that topological connectedness agrees exactly with accessibility by finite paths of unit lattice steps. We also present a deductive audit and the correspondence between this argument and a verification in Lean 4 and Mathlib, including…
items.summary: Constructs a topology on Z^n whose connected subsets are consecutive-integer sets, with the argument audited against a Lean 4 and Mathlib verification.

items.title: Order Maintenance in Worst-Case Constant Time, Verified
items.source_text: Order maintenance asks for a data structure that keeps a sequence of elements under insertions and deletions and tells which of two elements comes first. We give an algorithm, assembled from published components, that performs each operation in worst-case constant time, and verify it in Lean 4. The algorithm is a program for a random-access machine deeply embedded in Lean, whose interpreter counts every instruction. We prove that the program answers every query as a simple reference specification does, that each operation takes at most a fixed number of steps, independent of the number of…
items.summary: Presents an order maintenance algorithm with worst-case constant-time operations, verified in Lean 4 on a deeply embedded random-access machine model.

items.title: Preserving Separation Logic Specifications through Compilation
items.source_text: Program specifications in separation logic describe ownership of resources and serve as logical interfaces for local reasoning. Compiler correctness, expressed as semantics preservation, does not by itself supply such an interface for compiled code, because it does not explicitly relate source and target resources and assertions. We investigate WP-preserving compilation: when a compiler translates a source program, the weakest preconditions that the program satisfies in a separation logic carry over to the compiled program. Our proof technique consists of a resource-aware simulation over…
items.summary: Studies compilation that preserves separation logic weakest preconditions from source to compiled programs, using a resource-aware simulation proof technique.

items.title: Counting by the Book: Verifying Alaska's Ranked-Choice Elections
items.source_text: We present Alaska's ranked-choice elections as a case study in Formally Verified Democracy, a program to establish election results through formally checked proofs. We formalize an interpretation of Alaska's tabulation rules in Lean, verify its implementation, and prove election-specific results. Across 115 ranked-choice contests in Alaska since 2022, we identify 75 ballot records across 10 contests that were counted differently from this interpretation by a program reproducing the published results, without changing any winners. We trace these differences to overvotes and duplicate rankings…
items.summary: Formalizes Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation rules in Lean and verifies the implementation, finding 75 ballot records across 10 contests counted differently.

items.title: Reasoning about the Genetic Code in Lean
items.source_text: The genetic code exhibits redundancy, meaning that multiple distinct nucleotide sequences can encode the same amino acid sequence, a property mathematically characterized as non-injectivity. While this phenomenon is well studied in molecular biology, its rigorous verification within a computational framework remains limited. In this work, we present a machine-verified model of the central dogma of molecular biology using the Lean 4 interactive theorem prover. We formalize nucleic acid bases and amino acids as inductive types and define transcription and translation as functions mapping DNA…
items.summary: Presents a machine-verified model of the central dogma in Lean 4, formalizing bases, amino acids, transcription and translation to check genetic code…

items.title: count-catcher: Lean Theorems from Model Counting Certificates
items.source_text: We present count-catcher, a tool that turns a CPOG certificate of a count by the exact model counter d4 into a Lean theorem that a CNF formula defined in Lean has exactly N models over V variables. With an encoding lemma, this theorem becomes a theorem about the number of combinatorial objects. A CPOG certificate consists of a Boolean circuit equivalent to the formula and a proof of equivalence. count-catcher checks in Lean that the formula implies the circuit (forward check) and the circuit implies the formula (reverse check). For the forward check, lrat-catcher streams a refutation through…
items.summary: count-catcher turns CPOG certificates of d4 model counts into Lean theorems stating a CNF formula has exactly N models, with forward and reverse checks.

items.title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
items.source_text: Papers in statistical theory rest on long proofs that few readers check line by line. We present KAPPA (Kit of Agents for Proof-checking Papers with a proof Assistant), open-source software that organizes language model agents, run by Claude Code, to translate the proofs of a LaTeX paper into the proof assistant Lean 4 with its library Mathlib and check them there, result by result. Each numbered result receives one of four verdicts: verified unconditionally; verified conditionally, with every cited or unproved input stated as a named hypothesis; issue recorded, with its place in the paper…
items.summary: KAPPA is open-source software that uses language model agents to translate statistics paper proofs into Lean 4 with Mathlib and check them result by result.

items.title: Connecting Quantum Proof Systems and Hoare Logic
items.source_text: Verifying quantum programs today requires specialized proof systems built on interactive theorem provers such as Rocq, Lean, Isabelle, or Why3, and even modest quantum algorithms cost substantial human effort to verify. Because quantum programs cannot be effectively checked by runtime testing, formal verification is the only viable path to correctness, making the cost of these bespoke systems the chief barrier to scalable quantum software assurance. We show that verifying a quantum program should be no harder than verifying a classical array program, a paradigm commonly used in parallel…
items.summary: Proposes verifying quantum programs with Hoare-style array program reasoning instead of bespoke proof systems built on Rocq, Lean, Isabelle or Why3.

items.title: Efficient Proof Generation for Lean Statements with Multiple Candidate Answers
items.source_text: In formal systems such as Lean 4, efficiently finding answers to mathematical problems and generating verifiable proofs is an important task in automated mathematical reasoning. In the traditional way where an upstream solver provides multiple candidate answers, the common workflow requires searching for proofs for each candidate separately, incurring redundant computational cost. To this end, we propose a joint proof framework that integrates candidate answer selection, answer supplementation, and formal proof generation into a unified reasoning process. At its core is a trained prover that…
items.summary: A joint proof framework that selects candidate answers, supplements answers and generates formal Lean 4 proofs in one reasoning process.

items.title: Unit: a type checker for dependent type theory
items.source_text: We present Unit, a type checker for dependent type theory with a module system in the tradition of Automath and a uniform treatment of definitions. There is no unification, no instance search, no tactics and no unfolding heuristic, so the work of checking can be observed and compared with the informal proof. With Unit we have checked a model of univalent type theory, synthetic algebraic geometry, and synthetic Stone duality with its cohomology, and results in commutative algebra, like finite free resolutions and Zariski Main Theorem. These developments show that a small, uniform system…
items.summary: Unit is a type checker for dependent type theory with a module system, used to check developments including univalent type theory models and results in…

items.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
items.source_text: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are…
items.summary: Tests whether a simple agentic loop scaling test-time compute can match human-designed workflows for automated theorem proving in formal verification.

items.title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
items.source_text: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a…
